title: Fear not: the guru shows the way
hookLine: a student begs to be saved, and the teacher answers: fear not, and then, nobody can eat your dinner for you
carry: the guru shows the road; you walk it
tomorrow: The bee in the closing lotus

cards: The student arrives at the teacher's feet in a state. In the Vivekachudamani he describes himself as scorched, caught in the forest fire of the world, shaken by the winds of misfortune. He has no list of questions.
He has one request: save me. What a teacher says first, in that moment, shapes everything after. The book records it.
And a little later, it records something harder.

teach.h: FEAR NOT. THERE IS A WAY ACROSS.
teach.b: The guru's first words, in paraphrase: fear not, wise one. There is no danger for you. There is a way across this ocean, the way the sages crossed, and I will show it to you.
That's comfort, plainly given: you're not lost; there's a road. Then the student finds his questions. What is bondage?
How did it come? How does it stay? How do I get free?
The teacher praises him for asking. Then comes the harder part.

teach.h: A DEBT CAN BE PAID BY OTHERS.
teach.b: A father in debt, the text says, has sons and others to pay it off. But for bondage, there's no one to free you but yourself. Someone else can lift a heavy load from your head.

teach.h: HUNGER ENDS ONLY WHEN YOU EAT.
teach.b: Hunger, though, goes away only when you eat. A sick person gets well by taking the medicine and keeping to the diet, not by someone else doing it for them.
Later the text sharpens it: an illness isn't cured by saying the word medicine without drinking it. Fear not, and nobody can do this for you.

The book holds both: the teacher really can show the way, but can't walk it in the student's place. On this path, jnana isn't handed over like a parcel. It has to be eaten, so to speak, by the one who is hungry.
That's the Hindu bond of guru and disciple in one scene.

teach.h: HONOR THE GURU. DO YOUR SADHANA.
teach.b: It's why families touch a teacher's feet, and keep Guru Purnima, a full-moon day for thanking teachers: the guru lights the road.

teach.h: THE GURU SHOWS THE ROAD. YOU WALK IT.
teach.b: And it's why they still do their own sadhana, their daily practice: nobody can eat for them.

how: In Hindu practice the guru is honored deeply, with a bow or a touch of the feet, and on Guru Purnima, a full-moon day for thanking teachers; in Advaita Vedanta the guru is held to be essential for showing the way, while the student still reflects and meditates on the teaching personally until it becomes their own.

o: a store of facts gathered by reading many books
knowing that frees, which only the seeker can take in
the calm that comes after a good night's sleep

p: fear not, there is a way across
can be paid by sons and others

s: the teacher in the Vivekachudamani begins by scolding the student
his first words are comfort: fear not, there is no danger, there is a way across.
the text says someone else can pay your debts, but not free you from bondage
a father has sons to pay his debts, but for bondage there is no one but yourself.

games.q: you're the teacher. a student falls at your feet, scorched and frightened, and says: save me. what do you say first?
o: fear not. there is a way across, and I'll show it to you.
first, list everything you've done wrong.
I'll carry you across myself. you don't need to do anything.
games.why: the teacher begins with comfort: fear not, there is a way. later he adds that hunger ends only when you eat yourself.

practice: Bring to mind a teacher who showed you a way, a guru, a grandparent, anyone, and, as many Hindus do, bow to them inwardly in thanks.
Then bring to mind one thing you've been hoping someone else would fix for you, and hear the teacher: fear not, there is a way across.
Then ask, without scolding, what one small step on it is yours alone to take, and just see it clearly. If you pray, you can hold both the comfort and the step together.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani a teacher can show it, but like food or medicine, it works only for the one who takes it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: guru, teacher. In the Vivekachudamani the guru shows the way across, and the student walks it.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru shows the road; you walk it. Fear not, and nobody can eat your dinner for you. Day nine hundred ninety-five, done.
